name: Peer Review Best Practices
description: This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building peer review — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary peer review tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.
content:
This module lists the best, most commonly recommended practices for writing, implementing, and building peer review — the default, everyday guidance to apply on typical, ordinary peer review tasks and implementations, not specialized or unusual ones.

CORE GUIDELINES
1. Surface known limitations of a chosen peer review approach instead of presenting it as complete when it is not.
2. Prefer the simplest peer review approach that satisfies the requirement over a more general one that isn't needed yet.
3. Keep peer review outputs reproducible: fix seeds, record versions, and avoid hidden non-determinism where it matters.
4. Before starting peer review work, confirm the scope and constraints so the approach matches the actual requirement.
5. Document any non-obvious peer review decision with a short rationale so future readers understand the 'why', not just the 'what'.
6. Validate peer review outputs against a concrete example before treating the work as complete.
7. When multiple peer review strategies are viable, name the trade-off explicitly rather than silently picking one.
8. When peer review decisions are ambiguous, favor the option that is easiest to reverse or extend later.

COMMON PITFALLS TO AVOID
- Do not skip documenting peer review assumptions just because they seem obvious in the moment.
- Do not treat a single passing example as full verification of peer review correctness.
- Do not apply generic peer review advice without checking it fits the specific context at hand.
- Avoid introducing new peer review abstractions before there is a second concrete use case that needs them.
- Avoid mixing unrelated peer review concerns into a single change; keep each change focused.

CLOSING NOTE
These guidelines are a starting point for peer review, not an exhaustive rulebook — use judgment when a rule doesn't fit the situation.
